blocks.text: Aaron belongs to the Exodus and wilderness period in which Israel is formed through deliverance and covenant. The notice of his death and Eleazar's succession is therefore part of the chapter's remembered wilderness history, not an isolated biographical aside.

The succession from Aaron to his son Eleazar reflects a social world shaped by household ties, kinship duties, and organized religious life. The chapter connects that succession with Levi's continuing responsibilities for carrying the ark, ministering before the LORD, and blessing in his name, so family continuity and communal service appear together.

Deuteronomy moves from remembered wilderness history through covenant instruction to covenant consequences, renewal, succession, song, blessing, and Moses' death. Chapter 10 stands near the turn from recollection to sustained instruction: renewed tablets and wilderness events are recalled before Moses states what the LORD requires. One interpretive view understands the repeated commands in chapters 5-26 as covenant teaching rhetorically adapted for a successor generation rather than as mere word-for-word duplication of earlier laws. On that reading, this chapter applies inherited covenant instruction to people preparing to enter the land.
